newsitem.title: UK: Cold weather hampers deliveries of British beet.
newsitem.headline: Cold weather hampers deliveries of British beet.

text.p: Freezing temperatures across Britain's sugar beet growing areas are hampering deliveries into processing factories and a small percentage of the 1996/97 crop still remains to be lifted, British Sugar said on Wednesday.
While some beets had arrived frozen at factories, most deliveries were of good quality although delayed by the problems experienced by machinery lifting beets from hard ground.
"It's going pretty well, nobody's talking any serious damage to the beet crop at this stage. We're expecting an above average result," said a spokesman for British Sugar.
Five percent of the crop was still in the ground as at the end of last week, compared with four percent at the same stage in the 1995/96 campaign, he said.
Around 65 percent of beets had been delivered to factories compared with 72 percent in 1995/96.

Europe has recently seen the coldest weather in up to 30 years, with temperatures in the northern continent and eastern England -- where Britain's beet is mainly located -- hitting around minus 10 Celsius (14 Fahrenheit) at the end of last week.

"What we are seeing is with the persistent east winds, the beet that is being stored on farms in the south-east of the country...the clamps seem to have suffered more from the wind chill factor and the effects of penetrating frost," he said.
"With harvesting still continuing in areas where they can actually get a harvester on the land, beet is coming in frozen and the advice there is to deliver it into the factories."
British Sugar had advised beet growers to skim off the outer layers of frozen beet which could still be processed, he said.
But the risk was that frozen beet might be put into store where it could thaw and then re-freeze, making it turn into an unprocessable pulp.
Some 29 percent of the crop was in store on farms or in clamp, compared with 23 percent at the same stage last year. Sugar contents reached 17.7 percent for last week against 16.2 percent in 1996.
This year's campaign, expected to be complete by the end of February, started late to give beets more of a chance to develop and take advantage of mild autumn weather.
But the late start has meant more risk to the crop as a whole because a higher percentage has been at risk from frost.
"One would expect by now all the beet to be lifted and into store but obviously it will depend on the lifting conditions," said an official at the National Farmers Union (NFU).
